questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Velocity of a Particle at a Particular Moment
questions.problem: The displacement (in meters) of a particle moving in a straight line is given by the equation $s(t)={t}^{3}-{t}^{2}-15$ where $t$ is measured in seconds.  Find the velocity after $t=3\,\text{s}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the velocity function by differentiating the position function:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}-{t}^{2}-15) \\  & =3{t}^{2}-2t\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate the velocity at $t=3\,\text{s},$ we substitute $t=3$ into the velocity function above:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(3) & =3(3)^{2}-2(3) \\  & =27-6 \\  & =21\,\text{m/s}\end{aligned}
$$

provenance.kp_title: Calculating the Velocity of a Particle at a Particular Moment

questions.knowledge_point: Determining the Range of a Parametric Equation
questions.problem:
Given that a curve is defined parametrically as

$$
x=3-\frac{1}{2}t,\,y=\frac{3}{4}{t}^{2}-1,\,t\ge 2.
$$

Determine the ranges of $x$ and $y.$

$x$
{{field-1}}{{field-2}}$,\,y$
{{field-3}}{{field-4}}
questions.worked_solution:
Let's consider each variable in turn.

- To find the range of $x,$ note that $3-\frac{1}{2}t\le 2$ for all $t\ge 2.$ Consequently, the range of $x$ is

$$
x\le 2.
$$

- To find the range of $y,$ note that $\frac{3}{4}{t}^{2}-1\ge 2$ for all $t\ge 2.$ Consequently, the range of $y$ is

$$
y\ge 2.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Converting from Cartesian Coordinates to Polar Coordinates: Second or Third Quadrant
questions.problem:
A point $P$ has Cartesian coordinates $(-1,-1).$ Find the polar coordinates of $P.$ Give the polar angle in radians and do not round the answer.

The polar coordinates of $P$ are $(${{field-1}}$,$
{{field-2}}$).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we determine $r:$

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+1} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

For the reference angle, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{R} & =|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x})| \\  & =|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{-1}{-1})| \\  & =|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(1)| \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the point $P$ lies in the third quadrant, we add the reference angle to $\pi ,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta  & =\pi +{\theta }_{R} \\  & =\pi +\frac{\pi }{4} \\  & =\frac{5\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the polar coordinates of $P$ are  $(\sqrt{2},\frac{5\pi }{4}).$

provenance.kp_title: Converting from Cartesian Coordinates to Polar Coordinates: Second or Third Quadrant

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Three-Term Partial Fraction Decomposition
questions.problem:
Given that 

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}+31}{(x-2)^{2}(2x+1)}=\frac{A}{x-2}+\frac{B}{(x-2)^{2}}+\frac{C}{2x+1},
$$

where $A$, $B$, and $C$ are real constants, determine the value of $A\cdot B\cdot C.$
questions.worked_solution:
Multiplying both sides of the given equality by $(x-2)^{2}(2x+1)$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+31 & =A(x-2)(2x+1)+B(2x+1)+C(x-2)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Letting $x=-\frac{1}{2}$  gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{(-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+31 & =A(-\frac{1}{2}-2)(2[-\frac{1}{2}]+1)+B(2[-\frac{1}{2}]+1)+C{(-\frac{1}{2}-2)}^{2} \\ \frac{1}{4}+31 & =A(-\frac{5}{2})(-1+1)+B(-1+1)+C(\frac{25}{4}) \\ \frac{125}{4} & =\frac{25C}{4} \\ C & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

Letting $x=2$  gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{2}^{2}+31 & =A(2-2)(2\cdot 2+1)+B(2\cdot 2+1)+C(2-2)^{2} \\ 35 & =5B \\ B & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, letting $x=0$ and using our values for $B$ and $C$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{0}^{2}+31 & =A(0-2)(2\cdot 0+1)+7(2\cdot 0+1)+5(0-2)^{2} \\ 31 & =-2A+7+20 \\ 31 & =-2A+27 \\ 2A & =-4 \\ A & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

  

Hence,

$$
A\cdot B\cdot C=(-2)\cdot 7\cdot 5=-70.
$$

provenance.kp_title: Calculating a Three-Term Partial Fraction Decomposition

questions.knowledge_point: Integrating a Combination of Linear Rational Functions Using the General Formula
questions.problem: Calculate $\int (\frac{1}{5x+2}+\frac{1}{5x-2})\,\text{d}x.$ Assume that $K$ is an arbitrary positive constant.
questions.worked_solution:
Let's solve this using the general formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (\frac{1}{5x+2}+\frac{1}{5x-2})\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{5x+2}\,\text{d}x+\int \frac{1}{5x-2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡|5x+2|+\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡|5x-2|+C \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡|(5x+2)(5x-2)|+\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡K \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡(K|(5x+2)(5x-2)|)\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we used the laws of logarithms to write the result as a single logarithm.

provenance.kp_title: Integrating a Combination of Linear Rational Functions Using the General Formula

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying the Vertex of a Horizontal Parabola Given Its Graph

What is the vertex of the parabola shown above?
